terms.short: The rhythmic lift of jazz: long-short eighth notes and a pull against the beat.
terms.long: Swing is hard to define and easy to hear. The eighth notes are played unevenly, long then short, and the accents fall on the off-beats, so the music seems to lean forward while staying relaxed. It's also the name of the big-band era of the 1930s and 40s, when the whole country danced to it.

examples.note: Listen to the rhythm section under the riffs: the beat feels light and unstoppable.

terms.short: The composed melody, played at the start and again at the end of a performance.
terms.long: Most jazz performances follow the same shape: the band plays the tune (the head), soloists improvise over its chords, and the head comes back to close. Knowing that makes a long performance easy to follow.

examples.note: After the introduction, the bass asks and the horns answer: that call and response is the head.

terms.short: One time through a tune's form; solos are counted in choruses.
terms.long: In jazz a chorus isn't the refrain of a song: it's one complete pass through the tune's chord sequence, 12 bars for a blues, 32 for most standards. A soloist might take two choruses or twenty.

examples.note: Hawkins plays two choruses, and the second builds higher than the first.

terms.short: A tune's chord sequence, which the soloist improvises over.
terms.long: 'Playing the changes' means improvising lines that fit each chord as it goes by. Bebop made the changes faster and more complex; Giant Steps pushed them to an extreme, moving through three keys every few bars.

examples.note: The chords change every beat or two; Coltrane's lines spell out each one at full speed.

terms.short: The chords a pianist or guitarist plays behind a soloist, short for accompanying.
terms.long: Comping isn't just holding chords: good comping answers the soloist, leaves holes for them, and pushes the time with off-beat accents.

examples.note: Behind the horns, Kelly's bright, bluesy chord stabs are a conversation of their own.

terms.short: A bass line that moves one note per beat, outlining the chords.
terms.long: The walking bass gives swing its forward motion: four steady notes to the bar, stepping between the chord tones so the harmony is always clear.

examples.note: Under the solos Chambers walks, one note per beat, through the two modes.

terms.short: Soloists take turns playing four bars each, often with the drummer.
terms.long: Near the end of a performance, players often trade short phrases, usually four bars each, answering and challenging one another. With the drummer, it's a chance for drum solos in small doses.

examples.note: Toward the end, trumpet and drums trade short bursts at high speed.

terms.short: A moment when the band stops and one player fills the silence alone.
terms.long: Breaks go back to New Orleans, where a soloist would fill two bars while the band held still. A Night in Tunisia ends its interlude with a famous four-bar break.

examples.note: Listen for the band dropping out before the first solo: the trumpet bursts through the gap.

terms.short: The band plays only short accents, leaving the soloist exposed between them.
terms.long: In stop time the rhythm section hits one chord every bar or two and stays silent between, so the soloist has to carry the time alone.

examples.note: Armstrong's famous solo is played over stop-time hits: every bar, a chord, then only him.

terms.short: A short, repeated phrase, often played by one section behind another.
terms.long: Kansas City bands built whole arrangements from riffs: the saxophones repeat a figure, the brass answers with another, and the soloist rides on top.

examples.note: The saxophones' short repeated phrase is the riff the whole piece is built on.

terms.short: The loudest, fullest chorus of a big-band arrangement, near the end.
terms.long: The shout chorus is the climax of a big-band chart: the whole band plays together at full power, often in a new riff.

examples.note: Wait for the end, when the full band comes in together at full volume.

terms.short: One voice or section plays a phrase and another answers it.
terms.long: From African music, work songs and the church, call and response runs all through jazz, from riffing big bands to hard bop themes like Moanin'.

examples.note: The piano plays a phrase; the horns answer 'Amen'. That's the whole theme.

terms.short: A note bent flat, between major and minor: the sound of the blues.
terms.long: Blue notes, mostly the flattened third, fifth and seventh, sit between the cracks of the piano. Singers and horns bend into them; pianists suggest them by crushing two notes together.

examples.note: Smith's voice slides into and away from the notes: that bend is the blue note.

terms.short: The most common form in jazz: twelve bars on three chords, repeated.
terms.long: The blues form has three lines of four bars each, moving between the I, IV and V chords. Countless jazz tunes are blues, and players reharmonise it endlessly.

examples.note: Count along: every twelve bars, the form starts over.

terms.short: The shape of most standards: a section played twice, a contrasting bridge, then the first again.
terms.long: Most Broadway and Tin Pan Alley songs are 32 bars in four sections of eight: A, A again, a contrasting B (the bridge), and A to finish.

examples.note: Hear the opening melody twice, then a different section, then the opening again.

terms.short: The chords of Gershwin's I Got Rhythm, the second most used progression in jazz.
terms.long: After the blues, the most common chord sequence in jazz is the one from I Got Rhythm. Dozens of tunes, Lester Leaps In and Oleo among them, are new melodies over it.

examples.track: Count Basie's Kansas City Seven|Lester Leaps In
examples.note: Lester Young's tune is built on I Got Rhythm's chords: listen for the same bridge.

terms.short: A new melody written over an existing tune's chords.
terms.long: Bebop musicians wrote new themes over the chords of standards: Ornithology over How High the Moon, Ko-Ko over Cherokee. The new melody was theirs, and so were the royalties.

examples.note: A brand-new bebop line over the chords of How High the Moon.

terms.short: A short pattern repeated, often at the start or end of a tune, until the band moves on.
terms.long: A vamp holds a chord or two in a loop, to set a groove, wait for a soloist, or end a performance. Many modal and soul jazz tunes are built on vamps.

examples.note: The piano's repeated pattern is the vamp everything floats on.

terms.short: A figure repeated over and over beneath changing music.
terms.long: An ostinato is a stubborn repeated pattern, usually in the bass or piano. It holds the music in place while the solos move over it.

examples.note: Brubeck's left hand repeats the same two-chord pattern in five through the whole tune.

terms.short: Improvising on a scale held for many bars, instead of a fast chord sequence.
terms.long: In the late 1950s Miles Davis and others began to build tunes on one or two scales (modes) held for long stretches. With fewer chord changes, soloists had room to develop melody and mood.

examples.note: Sixteen bars on one scale, eight on another a half step up, then back: that's all the harmony.

terms.short: A slow tune, where tone and phrasing matter more than speed.
terms.long: Ballads show what a player sounds like: every note is exposed, and the art is in how long to hold it and where to place it.

examples.note: Coltrane plays his own ballad slowly over a held bass note, with almost no ornament.

terms.short: A piano style where the left hand leaps between bass notes and chords.
terms.long: Harlem stride, from the 1910s and 20s, grew out of ragtime: the left hand strides between a low bass note and a chord in the middle of the piano, while the right plays melody.

examples.note: Listen to the left hand jumping, low-high, low-high, under the melody.

terms.short: Improvised singing on nonsense syllables, like a horn solo.
terms.long: Scat turns the voice into an instrument. Louis Armstrong made it famous on record in 1926; Ella Fitzgerald made it an art.

examples.note: Halfway through, Armstrong drops the words and scats: the story goes he'd dropped the lyric sheet.
Fitzgerald's scat chorus quotes one tune after another.

terms.short: Coltrane's late-1950s torrents of fast notes, running up and down every chord.
terms.long: The critic Ira Gitler coined the phrase for John Coltrane's dense runs, played so fast that the notes blur into waves.

examples.note: In his solo Coltrane fills every beat with fast runs that sweep through the chords.

terms.short: The two-bar rhythmic key of Afro-Cuban music, which everything else fits around.
terms.long: Clave is a pattern of five strokes across two bars, played on wooden sticks or felt by everyone. In Afro-Cuban jazz the horns, piano and percussion all line up with it.

examples.note: The percussion lays down the Afro-Cuban groove before the horns come in on top.

terms.short: A device in the trumpet's bell that changes its sound.
terms.long: Mutes make the trumpet quieter and change its colour: the plunger for growls and wah-wahs, the Harmon for the close, metallic whisper of Miles Davis.

examples.note: Miles plays the melody through a Harmon mute: intimate and slightly buzzing.

terms.short: A rough, vocal sound made by humming or using a plunger mute while playing.
terms.long: Ellington's brass players made the horn talk: Bubber Miley and Cootie Williams growled through plunger mutes to create the band's 'jungle' sound.

examples.note: Williams switches between a plunger growl and an open, singing tone.

terms.short: Forcing a saxophone past its normal range into screams and multiple notes at once.
terms.long: Free and spiritual jazz saxophonists used overblowing to reach sounds beyond the instrument's normal notes: shrieks, honks and chords from a single horn.

examples.track: Pharoah Sanders|The Creator Has a Master Plan
examples.note: When the piece reaches its peak, Sanders's tenor turns to screams.

terms.short: Piano (or guitar), bass and drums: the players who keep the time and the harmony.
terms.long: The rhythm section is the engine of the band. Count Basie's, with Freddie Green, Walter Page and Jo Jones, was called the All-American Rhythm Section.

examples.note: Under the horns: Green's guitar chords on every beat, the walking bass, the light drums.

terms.short: The horns that play the melody and solos in a small band.
terms.long: In a hard bop quintet the front line is usually trumpet and saxophone, playing the head together in harmony or unison before taking solos.

examples.note: Trumpet and saxophone together in front, over Blakey's marching drums.

terms.short: An arrangement worked out by ear on the bandstand and never written down.
terms.long: Count Basie's band was famous for head arrangements: someone started a riff, the sections answered, and the piece took shape in the playing.

examples.note: The band's riffs were made up and memorised, not written: a head arrangement that became a hit.

terms.short: A tune every jazz musician is expected to know.
terms.long: Standards are the shared repertoire: Broadway and Tin Pan Alley songs, and jazz originals, that players can call at a session without rehearsing. The Songbook is a tour of them.

examples.track: Keith Jarrett, Gary Peacock & Jack DeJohnette|All the Things You Are
examples.note: A trio that spent thirty years reinventing standards like this one.

terms.short: Improvising without a fixed chord sequence, meter or form.
terms.long: From the late 1950s Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor and Albert Ayler let go of the changes, the steady beat, or both, and improvised from melody, energy and the other players.

examples.note: A folk-like melody, then a group improvising freely around it with no fixed beat.

terms.short: Several players improvising at once, each with a role.
terms.long: In New Orleans jazz the cornet leads, the clarinet weaves above, and the trombone slides below, all at once. Free jazz returned to the idea in the 1960s.

examples.track: King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band|Dipper Mouth Blues
examples.note: Two cornets, clarinet and trombone improvise together; each has its own lane.

terms.short: A jam session where players try to outplay each other.
terms.long: Stride pianists in Harlem and saxophonists in Kansas City competed in cutting contests, taking turns until one player was 'cut'. Speed, invention and stamina won.

examples.track: Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Bud Powell, Max Roach & Charles Mingus|Salt Peanuts
examples.note: Not a contest, but the spirit: bebop's masters taking turns at full tilt, live at Massey Hall.

howToListen.title: Find the beat
howToListen.text: Before anything else, tap your foot. The bass walks one note per beat; the drummer's ride cymbal keeps the pulse. Everything else happens against that time.

howToListen.title: Hear the tune
howToListen.text: The band starts with the melody, the head. Here the bass plays a phrase and the horns answer with two notes. Remember it: it'll come back.

howToListen.title: Follow the solos
howToListen.text: Then each player takes a solo over the tune's harmony, for a set number of choruses. Miles goes first, then Coltrane, then Cannonball Adderley, then Bill Evans.

howToListen.title: Listen to the conversation
howToListen.text: While one player solos, the others answer: the piano's chords push and prod, the drums react. Jazz is a band thinking together out loud.

howToListen.title: Hear the tune come back
howToListen.text: At the end the head returns, and the piece closes where it began, changed by everything that happened in between.
